prayer.text: Holy Spirit, protector of the Church, guide us into all truth.

cues.text: A Young Priest at a North African Council
In October 393, bishops of the Roman province of Africa gathered at Hippo Regius , the coastal city on the North African coast.

There, Augustine — not yet a bishop, only recently ordained a priest the previous year — had begun the ministry that would eventually make him the most influential theologian in the history of the Western Church.

Augustine himself was present among the assembled clergy, and preached before the council a discourse, De Fide et Symbolo , on the content of the Christian creed, one of his earliest surviving theological works.
Settling the Canon of Scripture
The council's most historically significant act was disciplinary rather than doctrinal in the technical sense.
It issued a formal list of the books recognized as belonging to Sacred Scripture.
The list enumerated twenty-seven books of the New Testament in exactly the form the Catholic Church has recognized ever since.

It was essentially the same list that Pope Damasus's Roman synod is believed to have promulgated a decade earlier, now formally adopted and confirmed by the bishops of an entire African province meeting in common council.
Other Disciplinary Business
Beyond the canon of Scripture, Hippo addressed ordinary African ecclesiastical discipline: regulating clerical conduct and the proper reception of penitents.

It also handled church order within the African provinces—the routine, unglamorous business of a regional council governing its own churches—which left a far thinner historical record than the canon list that would ultimately prove the council's most enduring legacy.
A Foundation Confirmed at Carthage
Hippo's ruling on the biblical canon did not stand alone; the same African bishops reconvened four years later at the neighboring Council of Carthage in 397.
There, they reaffirmed the identical list of twenty-seven New Testament books — a deliberate act of confirmation.
It gave the African Church's settled canon the added weight of a second, corroborating council rather than resting on Hippo's authority alone.
Legacy
Though Hippo's own acts survive today largely at second hand, referenced and summarized in later Carthage council records rather than preserved complete in their own right.
Its formal settlement of the New Testament canon marks one of the genuinely pivotal moments in the Bible's formation.
A specific, enumerated list of books, essentially identical to the one modern Catholics still read, first received a formal council's endorsement.
The young priest who would become Augustine of Hippo was among those present to witness it.
